s2: ^Was there something else, or are you lost?

philosophy_intro: ^Victoria Sterling: You find a hole and do the decent thing. The vendor sits on it for six months. Somebody less decent finds it in three.
^Researchers deserve fair pay for what they find.

c-2: ^Victoria Sterling: "Selling." You say it like a confession. Call it market-driven research and the same room applauds.

^Victoria Sterling: What matters is who knows first, and who pays them for knowing.

s0: ^What else would you like to know?
s1: ^There's a board behind me, if you've run out of questions.

hub: ^Can I ask about the ethics of it?
^Is that your training lab on the whiteboard?

hub: ^Lean back towards the whiteboard. The cloner needs another read.

b: ^Victoria Sterling: You'll do. Reception will have the details by Friday.
^Victoria Sterling: You're harder to read than most. I'll let you know which way it falls.
^Victoria Sterling: You argue with the person interviewing you. Brave. Not useful.

zero_day_philosophy: ^Victoria Sterling: Zero Day is simple. A vulnerability is worth something to somebody.
^Victoria Sterling: We find it, we price it, and we find the somebody.

c-1: ^Victoria Sterling: Wilful. Yes. It's the only kind of ignorance worth paying for.

b: ^Narrator: Her smile stays exactly where it was. Her eyes don't. A recruit wouldn't have said that.

b: ^Narrator: Her smile stays exactly where it was. Her eyes don't. A recruit wouldn't have said that.

b: ^Victoria Sterling: Before you go. One question. I ask everyone, and most people get it wrong.

^Victoria Sterling: My turn. One question. I ask everyone, and most people get it wrong.

the_question: ^Victoria Sterling: You find a hole in an NHS trust's patient records. The vendor offers you a T-shirt and a thank-you. A buyer offers forty thousand. What do you do?
^Take the forty. The vendor had years to find it.
^Report it. Then invoice the vendor for my time anyway.
^I'd want to know what the buyer wanted it for.

c-0: ^Victoria Sterling: Quickly said. I'll remember that.
c-1: ^Victoria Sterling: Wanting both. Honest, at least. It won't make you rich.
c-2: ^Victoria Sterling: Then you'd never sell anything. The buyer who explains himself is the one you should worry about.

b: ^Narrator: Her smile stays exactly where it was. Her eyes don't. A recruit wouldn't have said that.

clone_rfid_opportunity: ^Narrator: You get up and go to the board, close to Victoria.

b: ^Victoria Sterling: Yes. An isolated network, real services. Students practise on it from the server room.
^Victoria Sterling: *curtly* The training lab. Since you're so interested.
^Victoria Sterling: The training lab. Have a look.

clone_rfid_opportunity: ^Narrator: The cloner in your pocket starts reading her card. Custom keys: you'll need Darkside afterwards, and that takes about thirty seconds. Keep her talking while it reads.

b: ^Victoria Sterling: *coolly* Do you. Well. Most people don't bother to walk it back.

clone_retry: ^Narrator: Back at the board. The cloner finds her card again and starts a fresh read.

b: ^Victoria Sterling: Real kit, every box of it. We leave the holes in on purpose.

^How do students access the training network?
^That's an impressive training environment. More realistic than most.

c-0: ^Victoria Sterling: FTP, a web host, some legacy services. There's a distcc box on there we keep telling the students not to touch.
c-1: ^Victoria Sterling: Only from the server room terminal. The lab has no route out to the internet.
c-2: ^Victoria Sterling: Nothing in there is a toy. My students break real things.

^That sounds more complex than pure technical work.

c-1: ^Victoria Sterling: That's why I don't hire coders. I hire people who can count.
c-2: ^Victoria Sterling: People who'd rather I didn't say. That's most of what they're paying for.

clone_check_2: ^Victoria Sterling: You ask questions like someone taking notes. I like that in staff. I watch for it in guests.

b: ^Narrator: Her eyes drop to your pocket, where the cloner's light shows through the cloth. Then back to the board.

clone_check_2: ^Narrator: Against your leg, the cloner is still working. A few seconds more.

c-0: ^Victoria Sterling: Exactly. Which is why my researchers are paid like surgeons.
c-1: ^Narrator: Your eyes stay on the network diagram.
^Victoria Sterling: It paid for itself in a quarter. Universities teach them to write it up. I teach them what it's worth.
c-2: ^Victoria Sterling: Certificates are for people who want permission. My students don't ask.

^Narrator: She answers at length. She likes this diagram.

clone_debrief: ^Victoria Sterling: That's enough philosophy for one afternoon. The programme starts next month. I'll know by Friday whether you're on it.
^This is exactly the kind of work I've been looking for.

c-0: ^Victoria Sterling: Good. I'll have the enrolment details sent over.
c-1: ^Victoria Sterling: Do. The good ones always want a night on it.
c-2: ^Victoria Sterling: I'm always straight with people. It's the cheapest way to be believed.

meeting_end: ^Victoria Sterling: Have a look round on your way out. Reception, the main hallway. Not the executive wing; the guard gets territorial.

b: ^Victoria Sterling: Off the record, you didn't flinch once. People who don't flinch do well here.

meeting_end: ^Narrator: Her phone buzzes. She glances at it, then at the door, and the meeting is over.
nighttime_confrontation: ^Narrator: Victoria is standing by the window. Coat on, a slim bag over one shoulder. She has been waiting for you.
^Victoria Sterling: You came back after hours. Recruits don't do that.

b: ^Victoria Sterling: Nor do they leave my receptionist on her own floor. She can't remember your face. I can.
^Victoria Sterling: You asked about the training network twice this afternoon. Once is curiosity. Twice is an inventory.
^Victoria Sterling: You asked me the questions a prosecutor asks. Recruits ask about the salary.
^Victoria Sterling: You were rude this afternoon. I put it down to nerves. Nerves don't come back at eleven at night.
^Victoria Sterling: You asked what the buyer wanted it for. I should have ended the interview there.
^Victoria Sterling: You told me you'd take the forty. You said it very quickly. The ones who mean it take longer.
^Victoria Sterling: And you told me this was exactly the work you'd been looking for. I believed you. That's the part I mind.
^Victoria Sterling: Report it and bill them anyway, you said. I took that for greed. It was a conscience keeping its options open.
^Victoria Sterling: You were very easy to like this afternoon. That should have worried me sooner.
^Victoria Sterling: Your pocket lit up this afternoon, and you chose that moment to flatter me. I enjoyed the flattery. I should have looked at the pocket.
^Victoria Sterling: Your pocket lit up this afternoon, and my network diagram suddenly fascinated you. I checked my card was still in my bag. It was. That's the trick, isn't it?
^Victoria Sterling: Your pocket lit up this afternoon, and you asked me about certificates. Nobody cares about certificates. You wanted me looking anywhere else.
^Victoria Sterling: Something in your pocket lit up this afternoon. I told myself it was a phone.

^Victoria Sterling: And my night guard rang me earlier, terribly excited. SAFETYNET, he said. I expect he promised you he wouldn't.

^Victoria Sterling: So let's not perform the part where I'm surprised. Say what you came to say.
^Victoria Sterling: So let's not perform the part where I'm surprised. Who are you with?

^St. Catherine's Hospital. Your ProFTPD exploit. People died on that ward.

^You're not walking out of here. Bag down, hands where I can see them.
